chapters.title: Money, Markets, and Mankind
chapters.description: From clay tablets to quantum computers — the complete story of how humans learned to trade.

segments.text: Every trade ever made from a Mesopotamian farmer exchanging grain for bronze to an algorithm
firing 10,000 orders in the blink of an eye is a human story, a story of greed, ingenuity,
fear, and the relentless human desire to put a price on the future.
5,000 years ago, a Sumerian merchant pressed a reed into wet clay to record a promise.
Today, a server farm in New Jersey fires a micro-second order into a matching engine
before the light from your screen has even reached your eyes.
The technology changed.
The human impulse is behind it.
The hunger for profit, the terror of loss, the desperate need to know what something is
worth, those never changed at all.
This is the complete history of trading.
From clay tablets to quantum computers, from a button wood tree on Wall Street to a
Reddit form that shook Wall Street to its foundation.
From tulip bulbs that sold for the price of a canal house to a digital coin that turned
a $20 pizza order into what would have been a $690 million mistake.
Markets are not just economic systems.
They are civilization's most honest mirror reflecting everything we value.
Everything we fear and everything we're willing to bet on.
Pull up a chair.
The tape is running.

chapters.title: The First Traders
chapters.description: Mesopotamia, Phoenicians, Rome, and medieval fairs — the ancient roots of commerce.
chapters.keyFact: Sumerians invented cuneiform writing specifically to track trade contracts, 3000 BC

segments.text: Long before there were stock exchanges,
Bloomberg terminals or high frequency trading algorithms,
there were clay tablets.
In the river valleys between the Tigris and the Euphrates,
the region, the ancient Greeks would later call Mesopotamia,
meaning the land between the rivers were notorious.
Shhh.
Shhh.
Shhh.
First civilizations were grappling with a problem
that still drives markets today.
How do you record a promise?
I around 3,000 BC Sumerian merchants in cities like Uruk
and Uruk developed a writing system called Kunai Form,
not for poetry, not for prayer,
specifically to track commerce.
These were receipts.
Bills of lading, commodity contracts,
archaeologists have unearthed tens of thousands of clay tablets
describing grain deliveries, silver loans,
and forward contracts for goods to be delivered at a future date.
One famous tablet from roughly 1750 BC,
the code of Hammurabi,
includes laws governing interest rates,
debt, and commercial partnerships.
Shhh.
King Hammurabi was arguably the world's first financial regulator.
By 1,000 BC, the Phoenicians,
a sea-faring traders from what is now Lebanon,
had built the ancient world's most sophisticated trade network.
Their ships crossed the Mediterranean from Tyre and Scydon
to Carthage in North Africa to the coast of Spain,
and perhaps as far as Britain in search of tin.
What made them revolutionary wasn't just their seamanship.
They pioneered commercial credit,
lending goods against a future share of cargo profits.
They developed partnerships where one party provided capital
and another provided labor.
Sound familiar?
That's a limited partnership.
The Phoenicians were running hedge funds 3,000 years before
Greenwich Connecticut existed, then came Rome.
Walk through the forum in 100 AD
and you would find the world's most sophisticated
commercial ecosystem.
Roman bankers, the Argentinei,
operated permanent booths in the forums,
accepting deposits, making loans,
and exchanging foreign currencies.
The Romans even developed a form of corporate share.
The Pueblacani, private companies that contracted to build roads
and supply the Roman army,
issued shares called parties that traded in the form Romanum.
Cicero himself, writing around 70 BC,
mentions these shares changing hands.
Rome had a stock market.
It didn't survive the fall of the empire,
but the idea did.
Fast forward to 12th century France.
The champagne fairs rotating through six towns
on a carefully scheduled calendar
became the commercial hub of medieval Europe.
Italian merchants invented the Bill of Exchange,
a written promise to pay a specific sum
in a specific currency at a future date and location.
No gold needed to change hands at the fair.
Credit could be extended across thousands of miles
and settled months later.
The medieval Italians had invented financial abstraction
and with it the DNA of the modern financial system.

chapters.title: The Birth of the Stock Market
chapters.description: The VOC, Amsterdam's Beurs, tulip mania, and the Buttonwood Agreement that founded the NYSE.
chapters.keyFact: VOC 1602: the world's first publicly traded corporation, valued higher than most nation-states

segments.text: On March 20, 1602, the Dutch states general granted a charter to a new enterprise, the Verenig
de Ust Indische Komponie, the Dutch East India Company, history knows it by three letters,
VOC. The VOC was, by any measure, the most powerful corporation that has ever existed.
At its peak, it employed 50,000 workers, operated 150 merchant ships and 40 warships,
minted its own coins, negotiated treaties with foreign governments, and maintained private
armies across Asia. Its revenues exceeded those of several European nation states combined.
It was a sovereign commercial empire with shareholders. Those shareholders approximately 1143 of them
in the initial offering could trade their shares on the Amsterdam Burs, the world's first
formal stock exchange, established in 1611. For the first time, ownership of a company was separated
from management. For the first time, an ordinary merchant in Amsterdam could become a partial
owner of a spice route halfway around the world. The concept of the publicly traded corporation,
arguably the most powerful organizational invention in human history's halls,
was born in the Netherlands four centuries ago. The Amsterdam Exchange developed with breath
taking sophistication. By the 1630s, traders were executing forward contracts and options on VOC
shares. Drivatives that allowed speculation on future prices without owning the
underlying shares. Sound familiar? It should. Joseph De La Vega published a book in 1688,
describing the Amsterdam market's bulls, bears, shortsellers, and crowd psychology.
It reads like a description of modern Wall Street, but Amsterdam also gave us Tulip Mania,
the world's first recorded speculative bubble, and the template for every bubble that followed.
Tulips, introduced from the Ottoman Empire in the 1550s, had become a luxury status symbol
by the mid 1630s. Futures contracts on tulip bulbs were trading in taverns across the Dutch Republic.
At the Bubbles Peak in January 1637, a single bulb of the Semper Augustus variety reportedly sold
for 10,000 guilders, the price of a fine Amsterdam canal house. Then, in February 1637,
buyers stopped showing up. Prices collapsed within days. The pattern would repeat, south
sea company stock in 1720. Railroad shares in the 1840s, technology stocks in 1999.
Mortgage-backed securities in 2007, the asset changes, the psychology doesn't. Meanwhile,
in London, the coffee house was giving birth to what would become the world's greatest financial
empire. Jonathan's coffee house from 1698 was where stock and commodity brokers gathered,
posted prices on the walls, and struck deals with hand shakes. In 18...
401, they moved into a purpose-built building and called themselves the stock exchange.
On May 17, 1792, 24 brokers in New York signed the Buttonwood Agreement under a tree on Wall Street
and founded American Capitalism.

chapters.title: Ticker Tape and Telegrams
chapters.description: The telegraph, the stock ticker, J.P. Morgan, and the first information arms race.
chapters.keyFact: Edison sold his improved stock ticker for $40,000 in 1869 — seed money for Menlo Park

segments.text: On May 24, 1844, Samuel Moore sent the first long distance telegraph message from Washington
to Baltimore.
What Gary and Gary is what, what have God wrought?
Within a decade where the financial implications were profound.
Before the telegraph, market information traveled at the speed of horses, ships, and messengers.
Prices in New York might not be known in Philadelphia for hours.
The price of cotton in New Orleans was unknown in London for weeks.
Geographic arbitrage, buying low here and selling high there.
Was a legitimate and lucrative business.
Simply because no one knew what things cost anywhere else.
The telegraph collapsed those asymmetries by the 1850s telegraph lines linked every
major American city.
By 1866, a transatlantic cable connected New York to London.
The trader with telegraph access had an enormous advantage over the one without.
This was the first iteration of what traders would always want, an information edge.
The arms race that began with Samuel Morris has never stopped, then came the ticker.
On November 15, 1867, a 22-year-old named Edward Callahan demonstrated the stock ticker
in New York.
A telegraphic receiver that automatically printed stock, symbols, prices, and volumes on a continuous
strip of narrow paper.
It was the first real-time financial data feed.
Before Callahan's invention, brokers outside the exchange had to wait for runners.
I'm literally young men sprinting through the streets to deliver price updates.
Thomas Edison, 21 years old and already celebrated, saw the ticker and said about improving it.
In 1869, he sold his improved version to the Golden Stock telegraph company for $40,000.
That money funded his research laboratory at Menlo Park, the stock market financed
the invention of the light bulb.
By the 1880s, ticker machines were standard in every brokerage, house, bank,
and hotel lobby in America.
Crowds gathered in front of brokerage windows to watch the tape roll by.
When Charles Lindbergh returned from his transatlantic flight in 1927, New York shower,
shower him with used ticker tape.
Ticker tape parade entered the language and then came JP Morgan.
No figure, better embodies the gilded age of American finance.
Born in 1837, Morgan Wood, by the turn of the 20th century, exercise more personal control over
the American financial system than any man before or since.
He assembled US Steel in the first billion dollar corporation in American history
by buying Andrew Carnegie's empire for $480 million.
He controlled railroads representing one-sixth of the nation's total mileage.
And in 1907, when a banking panic gripped the country, no federal reserve existed yet.
Morgan locked the nation's bank presidents in his Madison Avenue library
and refused to let them leave until they had pooled their resources to stabilize the system.
He was a one-man central bank.
Markets survived.
But the episode made clear the era of personal financial empires had to end.

chapters.title: The Great Crash
chapters.description: Black Thursday 1929, the Great Depression, margin calls, and how the SEC and Glass-Steagall rebuilt the system.
chapters.keyFact: $30 billion in market value wiped out in 48 hours — the Dow fell 89% from 1929 peak to 1932 trough

segments.text: The 1920s were a decade of intoxicating prosperity
and dangerous financial excess.
Between 1920 and 1929,
the Dow Jones industrial average rose more than 500%.
But the gains were built on margin.
Investors could buy stocks by putting up as little as 10%
of the purchase price and borrowing the rest.
At 10 to 1 leverage, a 10% move in the stock price
doubled your money or wiped you out completely.
By 1929, margin debt had reached staggering levels.
Brokerages were lending freely.
Banks were lending to brokerages.
Everyone was leveraged, everyone was bullish,
and the market had become disconnected
from economic reality.
The crack appeared on October 24th, 1929.
Black Thursday.
Trading volume overwhelmed the ticker tape system.
The tape ran hours behind,
leaving brokers and investors trading blind,
unable to get accurate prices.
A wave of selling hit the market.
Bankers pooled resources to attempt a stabilization.
Echoes of 1907, but it bought only days.
On Monday, October 28th, the Dow fell 12.8%.
On Tuesday, October 29th, Black Tuesday,
I went, fell another 11.7% in two days,
$30 billion in market value.
It evaporated.
That's roughly $500 billion in today's money.
Wipeed out in 48 hours.
By the summer of 1932, the Dow had fallen 89%
from its 1929 peak.
Thousands of banks failed.
Unemployment reached 25%.
The Great Depression had begun.
The crash exposed the complete absence of market regulation.
There was no deposit insurance.
No agency overseeing securities markets.
No requirement for companies to disclose their finances.
It was the financial equivalent of flying blind.
Franklin Roosevelt's response
reshaped American finance for a generation.
The Glass Stagall Act of 1933 drew a bright line
between commercial banking, taking deposits
and making loans and my worry and investment banking,
underwriting and trading securities.
JP Morgan and company had to choose.
They split into two firms.
JP Morgan, the commercial bank and Morgan Stanley,
the investment bank.
The banking act of 1933 created the federal
deposit insurance corporation.
The FDIC, guaranteeing deposits up to $2,500 per account.
For the first time, ordinary Americans didn't have
to worry that their bank would fail
and take their savings with it.
And in 1934, Congress created the Securities
and Exchange Commission, the SEC,
to regulate the securities markets that had self-destructed
Roosevelt appointed Joseph Kennedy,
a notorious market manipulator himself,
as its first chairman on the theory
that it takes a thief to catch a thief.
These reforms defined American finance for the next 65 years.
Some would argue they defined it too well.
They're undoing in 1999 would help set the stage
for an even greater reckoning.

chapters.title: The Electronic Revolution
chapters.description: NASDAQ 1971, the Bloomberg Terminal, the dot-com retail trading boom, and Black Monday's automated cascade.
chapters.keyFact: Black Monday Oct 19, 1987: 22.6% single-day Dow drop — still the largest one-day percentage decline in history

segments.text: On February 8, 1971, the National Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation
System, Nasdaq, went live.
It was the world's first electronic stock market.
Nasdaq didn't have a trading floor.
No specialists, no hand signals, no paper tickets.
Instead, market makers were connected by a computer network.
Any broker in the country could see the best available quotes instantly.
The exchange was philosophical as much as technological.
Nasdaq's competing market maker model dispersed price making power across dozens of firms
instead of concentrating it in a few designated specialists.
The debate about which model produced better prices, more competition or concentrated
liquidity would fuel 30 years of arguments.
Nasdaq was created for smaller growth-oriented companies.
Its early technology listings included Intel, listed in 1971, and Apple, listed in
By the 90s, Nasdaq was the natural home of the digital economy.
Then, in 1981, Michael Bloomberg recently fired from investment bank Salomon Brothers
with a $10 million severance package founded a financial data company with a radical premise,
give traders not just data, but analysis.
The Bloomberg Terminal launched in 1982, delivered real-time prices, news, and analytical
tools that let traders calculate yields and compare securities without calling a research
analyst.
Information that had been locked in the heads of specialists was suddenly on every trading
desk.
By 2000, there were over 100,000 Bloomberg Terminals worldwide.
By 2024, 330,000, each one running roughly $25,000 a year, Bloomberg LP's annual revenue
now exceeds $6 billion dollars, the severance from Salomon Brothers may be the greatest
return on investment in financial history, meanwhile, the dark side of automation was becoming
visible.
On the morning of October 19, 1987, the Dow Jones industrial average opened and began to
fall.
By the close, it had dropped 508 points, a 22.6% decline in a single session.
The largest single-day percentage drop in market history.
$500 billion in value vanished in six hours.
The approximate cause was portfolio insurance, computer programs that automatically sold
stock index futures as the market declined, theoretically limiting losses.
In practice, on that morning, thousands of computers simultaneously began selling futures.
The selling drove prices lower, which triggered more automatic selling.
No circuit breakers existed.
There was no mechanism to pause the cascade.
Black Monday was the first catastrophic failure caused by automated trading strategies interacting
in unintended ways.
What technologists would later call emergent behavior of a complex system.
It would not be the last.
Markets recovered.
But the event had revealed something important.
Markets had become machines.
And machines could malfunction in ways their designers had not anticipated.

chapters.title: The Quant Invasion
chapters.description: Renaissance Technologies, D.E. Shaw, the dot-com bubble, and LTCM's $4.6 billion collapse.
chapters.keyFact: Renaissance Medallion Fund: 66% average annual returns before fees since 1988 — no other fund comes close

segments.text: The 1990s internet boom transformed retail investing as profoundly as the telegraph had
transformed professional trading a century earlier.
Before online brokers placing a stock trade meant calling a broker who charged a full service
commission, often $100 or more per trade.
By 1999, E-trade was charging $14.95 online.
E-trade dropped to $8.
The barriers to stock market participation had collapsed.
Day trading, buying and selling stocks multiple times within a single session became a cultural phenomenon.
In 1999, it was estimated that 100,000 Americans were full-time day traders.
Day trading academies opened in strip malls, books with titles like How I Made 2 Million Day
trading stocks became best sellers.
The democratization of trading had arrived just in time for one of the greatest speculative bubbles
in financial history.
By 1999, the NASDAQ composite index had risen 400% in five years.
Technology stocks were trading at price to earnings ratios of 100, 200, sometimes infinity,
companies with no earnings at all.
Pets.com raised $82 million in an IPO in February 2000.
The logic was new economy thinking.
The internet changes everything.
Traditional valuation metrics don't apply.
If you don't invest now, you'll be left behind.
Every generation's bubble has its own rationalization for why this time is different.
The NASDAQ peaked at 5,048 on March 10, 2000.
Then it began to fall.
By October 2002, it had lost 78% of its value.
$3 trillion in market capitalization had evaporated.
But while retail traders were day trading pets.com,
something more consequential was happening in the quantitative hedge funds.
Jim Simons was a mathematician and former NSA codebreaker who founded
Renaissance Technologies in 1982.
His medallion fund employs only scientists, mathematicians, and computer scientists,
no economists, no finance MBAs.
Since 1988, it has generated average annual returns of 66% before fees over 35 years.
That is a track record no other fund in history has come close to matching.
De Shaw founded in 1988 by a Columbia computer science professor.
Was one of the first firms to systematically apply computational methods to stock picking.
One of its senior vice presidents tasked with exploring opportunities in the nascent
worldwide web left in 1994 to start his own company.
His name was Jeff Bezos.
Then in 1998, Wall Street received a warning it would largely choose to ignore.
Long-term capital management, a hedge fund founded by a legendary bond trader
and two Nobel Prize-winning economists had accumulated $1.25 trillion in leverage positions.
When Russia defaulted on its debt in August 1998,
LTCM lost $4.6 billion in four months.
The Fed coordinated a $3.6 billion bailout.
The lesson was stark.
Mathematical models built on historical data cannot account for events they have never observed.
Leverage can turn a bad bet into an existential catastrophe.
Wall Street would need to learn this lesson again at much greater cost.

chapters.title: The Speed Wars
chapters.description: HFT, co-location, the Flash Crash of 2010, and dark pools — the hidden market.
chapters.keyFact: Spread Networks spent $300M drilling through mountains for a 4-millisecond trading edge Chicago to New York

segments.text: In 2005, the Securities and Exchange Commission passed regulation national market system,
reg NMS, with the laudable goal of ensuring investors always received the best available price
across all exchanges.
The unintended consequence, Reg NMS created the conditions for high-frequency trading to flourish.
If the best price must always be executed first, then the firm that could get to that best
price fastest, faster than any other firm, would have a structural, systematic advantage.
The race was on, not in hours, not in minutes, in micro seconds.
High-frequency trading firms invested hundreds of millions of dollars to shave micro seconds
off execution times.
They paid exchanges to house their servers in the same data centers as the exchange
matching engines, connected by the shortest possible cable lengths.
They laid private, fiber-optic cables across the country.
In 2010, a company called Spread Networks completed a straight line fiber cable from Chicago
to New York, drilling through mountains rather than following existing rights of way to
reduce round-trip communication time from 17 milliseconds to 13.1 milliseconds.
The project cost $300 million.
The four millisecond advantage it provided was worth hundreds of millions in trading profits.
Four milliseconds.
$300 million.
By 2012, high-frequency trading firms accounted for roughly 50% of all equity trading volume
in the United States.
They weren't predicting where prices were going.
They were simply being faster than everyone else at responding to where prices were right
now.
And then, on May 6, 2010, the system showed exactly what it was capable of.
At 2.32 in the afternoon, the Dow Jones industrial average already down 300 points on the day began
falling at a rate that had no precedent.
Within 14 minutes, it had fallen an additional 600 points.
Total intraday decline nearly 1,000 points, nearly $1 trillion in market value had evaporated.
Then 20 minutes later, it was almost entirely back.
Investigators later found that a single mutual fund had entered a $4.1 billion sell order
in S&P 500 futures using an algorithm set to execute regardless of price or time.
HFT algorithms detecting the selling pressure pulled their orders.
The market became illiquid.
Prices went into freefall.
Accenture.
A company worth $35 billion briefly traded at one penny per share.
Apple briefly traded at $100,000 per share.
These were not real trades.
They were the artifacts of algorithms executing in a vacuum.
The flash crash was the most visible demonstration yet that the market had become a machine.
A machine whose behavior, under stress, could not be reliably predicted by anyone, including its designers.

chapters.title: The 2008 Reckoning
chapters.description: CDOs, Lehman Brothers' $613B bankruptcy, AIG's $440B CDS exposure, and the $700B TARP bailout.
chapters.keyFact: $22 trillion in lost economic output — the total cost of the 2008 financial crisis

segments.text: In September 2008, the global financial system came closer to total collapse than at any
point since the 1930s.
The story began with a deceptively simple idea.
Pool thousands of home mortgages together, sell them as bonds to investors worldwide, and
in everyone profits, as long as housing prices keep rising.
The model worked until it didn't.
The problem was subprime mortgages, years-yurczur, zine, loans made to borrowers with poor credit
histories sold by aggressive lenders who collected their fees and passed the risk to someone else.
Those loans were bundled into mortgage-backed securities, then repackaged into collateralized
debt obligations, CDOs, sliced into tranches of supposedly varying risk.
The magic trick, by pulling enough risky mortgages, you could supposedly manufacture AAA-rated
securities.
The rating agencies, Moody's standard and poor's, Fitch blessed the mathematics.
They were catastrophically wrong.
Credit default swaps, insurance contracts on bond defaults created a web of interconnected
obligations across the entire financial system.
AIG, the insurance giant, had sold $440 billion in credit default swaps, guaranteeing mortgage
bonds held by nearly every major financial institution on earth.
When those bonds defaulted, AIG couldn't pay.
The US government provided an $85 billion emergency bailout to AIG in September 2008,
effectively bailing out every counterparty simultaneously.
On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers, with $613 billion in debt, filed for bankruptcy,
the largest bankruptcy in US history.
The next day a money market fund holding Lehman paper broke the buck.
Its share price fell below $1.
A run on money market funds began.
Credit markets froze.
The commercial paper that businesses needed for day-to-day operations stopped flowing.
The entire financial system was seizing up.
Congress passed the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program tarp to stabilize the
banking system.
The Federal Reserve cut interest rates to near zero.
The Fed's balance sheet expanded from less than $1 trillion to over $4 trillion.
The total cost of the 2008 crisis has been estimated at $22 trillion in lost economic output.
$10 trillion in lost household wealth.
$8.7 million American jobs.
$22 trillion.
The 2010 Dodd-Frank Act attempted to rebuild the regulatory framework.
New capital requirements for banks is an oversight of derivatives markets.
A consumer financial protection bureau.
The repeal of Glass-Steagall, which had separated commercial and investment banking since 1933,
was widely cited as one of the structural preconditions for what happened.
Wall Street, as always, was already looking forward.
But history had a way of demanding to be remembered.

chapters.title: Bitcoin and the Blockchain Revolution
chapters.description: Satoshi Nakamoto's whitepaper, Bitcoin Pizza Day, Ethereum smart contracts, DeFi summer, and the FTX collapse.
chapters.keyFact: 10,000 BTC bought two pizzas in 2010 — at Bitcoin's 2021 peak, that was $690 million worth of pizza

segments.text: On October 31, 2008, two weeks after Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, a person or
persons using the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto posted a nine-page paper to a cryptography
mailing list.
The paper was titled, Bitcoin appeared to peer electronic cash system.
The timing was not coincidental.
Bitcoin's proposition was, in part, a direct response to the crisis unfolding around it.
What if you could transfer value directly between two parties without trusting a bank,
a payment processor, or any other intermediary?
What if cryptographic proof replaced institutional trust?
The Bitcoin network went live on January 3, 2009.
Nakamoto mined the first block, embedding in it a headline from that day's times of London,
Chancellor, on brink of second bailout for banks.
The political statement was explicit.
Bitcoin first traded on exchanges in 2010.
The famous first real-world transaction used 10,000 BTC worth roughly $41 at the time to
buy two pizzas from a Jacksonville, Florida, Papa Johns.
Those 10,000 Bitcoin at Bitcoin's 2021 peak of $69,000 would have been worth $690 million.
The pizza buyer's name is Laslo Hanyech.
May 20, T-Tune is celebrated in the crypto community as Bitcoin pizza day.
Laslo does not talk about it much.
In July 2015, Vitalik Booterin launched Ethereum, a programmable blockchain.
Its key innovation was smart contracts, self-executing programs that live on the blockchain,
and automatically execute the terms of an agreement when predetermined conditions are met.
No intermediary, no lawyer, just code.
By the summer of 2020, decentralized finance had arrived.
DeFi protocols, Uniswap, Compound, Avae, MakerDow.
We're building replicas of traditional financial services entirely on blockchain infrastructure.
No company, no bank, no intermediary.
Total value locked in DeFi exploded from less than $1 billion to over $15 billion in a matter of months.
By 2021, DeFi protocols held over $100 billion then came the NFT mania.
Digital artwork selling for tens of millions of dollars.
Profile pictures with legal ownership on the blockchain.
Critics called it madness.
Believers called it the future of ownership.
Then Bitcoin fell 80%.
Then Ethereum fell 80%.
Then FTX, one of the largest crypto exchanges in the world,
collapsed in a matter of days in November 2022 with founder Sam Bankman Fried facing criminal charges
for misappropriating customer funds.
The pattern was achingly familiar.
Tulip Mania, southcbubble.com, 2008, now crypto.
An asset with genuine but limited intrinsic value driven to irrational heights by speculation,
collapsing when the music stopped.
And then as always, these survivors rebuilt.
BlackRock launched a tokenized money market fund on Ethereum in March 2024.
The technology remained.
The speculation eventually had to reckon with reality.

chapters.title: GameStop and the Meme Revolution
chapters.description: Reddit's WallStreetBets, the GameStop short squeeze, Melvin Capital's $6.8B loss, and the democratization of market power.
chapters.keyFact: GameStop rose 2,300% in 3 weeks — from $20 to $483 — driven by Reddit retail traders

segments.text: On January 27, 2021, something happened that Wall Street had not anticipated.
Retail investors on Reddit organized.
GameStop, a struggling video game retailer, had been heavily short-sold by hedge funds,
particularly Melvin Capital, which held a massive position betting the stock would fall.
Members of the Reddit forum, RG Wall Street, Bets, numbering in the millions, organized
a coordinated buying campaign to force a short squeeze.
Driving GameStop's stock price up fast enough to force the short sellers to cover their positions
at enormous losses.
GameStop's stock rose from $20 in early January to an intraday high of $483 on January 28th,
a 2300% increase in less than a month.
Melvin Capital lost $6.8 billion.
When Robin Hood, the Commission-free trading app beloved by the Reddit traders,
briefly halted buying of GameStop shares on January 28th,
citing liquidity concerns, the fury of retail investors exploded across the internet.
Congressional hearings were convened.
Robin Hood's CEO testified.
GameStop was about more than one stock.
It was about the democratization of market power.
The realization that millions of coordinated small investors,
armed with Commission-free apps and social media coordination,
could challenge the dominance of billion-dollar hedge funds.
It was also a reminder that markets are social systems as much as economic ones,
and that social media had changed the information environment of financial markets
in ways that regulators, institutions, and academic finance had not begun to fully reckon with.
The little guy had always been in the market.
This was the first time the little guys got together in a room,
a very large, very chaotic digital room, and decided to make the big guys feel it.

chapters.title: Trading in 2030
chapters.description: AI autonomous trading agents, quantum computing arms race, tokenized assets at $16T, CBDCs, and 24/7 markets.
chapters.keyFact: McKinsey estimates tokenized asset markets reach $16 trillion by 2030

segments.text: We are entering an era in which trading decisions are not merely assisted by artificial intelligence.
They are made by it.
Autonomous AI trading agents, software systems that perceive market conditions,
formulate strategies, execute trades, and learn from outcomes without human intervention.
Are moving from research labs into production.
Unlike traditional quantitative strategies that follow fixed rules derived from historical data,
next-generation AI agents use reinforcement learning.
Discovering trading strategies by trial and error in simulated and live market environments.
They adapt to changing market conditions without being explicitly reprogrammed.
By the 2020s, AI-driven funds were analyzing everything from satellite imagery of retail parking lots
and shipping port congestion to credit card transaction data, job postings, and social media sentiment.
In 2023 and 2024, large language models began analyzing earnings calls, SEC filings,
and central bank statements in real time, extracting signals faster than any human analyst.
The question was no longer whether AI could analyze markets.
It was whether human judgment added any value at all.
Quantum computing is the next arms race.
IBM, Google, and IonQ have demonstrated quantum computers with increasing power.
Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan have active quantum research divisions.
The consensus useful quantum advantage in financial applications is likely five to ten years away,
but the investment is happening now.
Because the firm that gets there first could achieve an information and computational advantage
that makes every previous arms race look like a footnote.
Meanwhile, the infrastructure of markets itself is being rebuilt.
BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager with $10 trillion under management,
launched a tokenized money market fund on the Ethereum blockchain in March 2024.
JP Morgan processes billions in tokenized repo transactions daily.
McKinsey estimates that by 2030, the total tokenized asset market could reach $16 trillion.
Real estate, government bonds, corporate credit, private equity, all of it fractional,
tradable, settling in seconds instead of two business days.
Over 130 countries representing 98% of global GDP
